section.title: The Birth of Samson
section.sectionRationale: The last and longest of the judge stories opens not with a battle but with a birth. Israel has sunk again into evil, and this time God does not even wait for them to cry out; unbidden, He sends the Angel of the LORD to a barren woman in Zorah to announce a son who will be a Nazirite from the womb and begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. The chapter is a sustained theophany, awe-filled and tender, in which the mysterious visitor whose name is Wonderful ascends in the altar flame. It is one whole movement: grace announcing a deliverer before the deliverer draws a breath.
section.thesis: Into a season so dark that Israel no longer even cries for help, God graciously takes the initiative, sending the Angel of the LORD to a barren woman to promise and set apart a deliverer from the womb; the Nazirite child is God's gift, and the awesome visitor whose name is Wonderful, worshiped in the ascending flame, unveils the God who stoops to save an undeserving people.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the Angel's announcement to the barren woman, verses 1 to 7; Manoah's prayer and the Angel's return, verses 8 to 14; the offering, the ascending flame, and the name Wonderful, verses 15 to 23; and the birth of Samson and the stirring of the Spirit, verses 24 to 25.

units.label: The Angel announces a son to the barren woman
units.note: a Nazirite to God from the womb

verses.text: Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD, so He delivered them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.
Now there was a man from Zorah named Manoah, from the clan of the Danites, whose wife was barren and had no children.
The angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, “It is true that you are barren and have no children; but you will conceive and give birth to a son.
Now please be careful not to drink wine or strong drink, and not to eat anything unclean.

For behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son. And no razor shall touch his head, because the boy will be a {{nazir|Nazirite}} to God from the womb, and he will begin the deliverance of Israel from the hand of the Philistines.”
So the woman went and told her husband, “A man of God came to me. His appearance was like the angel of God, exceedingly awesome. I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name.

But he said to me, ‘Behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son. Now, therefore, do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb until the day of his death.’”

units.label: Manoah's prayer and the Angel's return
units.note: teach us how to raise the boy

verses.text: Then Manoah prayed to the LORD, “Please, O Lord, let the man of God You sent us come to us again to teach us how to raise the boy who is to be born.”
And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the {{malak|angel}} of God returned to the woman as she was sitting in the field; but her husband Manoah was not with her.
The woman ran quickly to tell her husband, “Behold, the man who came to me the other day has reappeared!”
So Manoah got up and followed his wife. When he came to the man, he asked, “Are you the man who spoke to my wife?” “I am,” he said.
Then Manoah asked, “When your words come to pass, what will be the boy’s rule of life and mission?”
So the angel of the LORD answered Manoah, “Your wife is to do everything I told her.
She must not eat anything that comes from the vine, nor drink any wine or strong drink, nor eat anything unclean. She must do everything I have commanded her.”

units.label: The ascending flame and the name Wonderful

verses.text: “Please stay here,” Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, “and we will prepare a young goat for you.”
And the angel of the LORD replied, “Even if I stay, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD.” For Manoah did not know that it was the angel of the LORD.
Then Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, “What is your name, so that we may honor you when your word comes to pass?”
“Why do you ask my name,” said the angel of the LORD, “since it is {{pele|beyond comprehension}}?”
Then Manoah took a young goat and a grain offering and offered them on a rock to the LORD. And as Manoah and his wife looked on, the LORD did a marvelous thing.
When the flame went up from the altar to the sky, the angel of the LORD ascended in the flame. When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell facedown to the ground.
And when the angel of the LORD did not appear again to Manoah and his wife, Manoah realized that it had been the angel of the LORD.
“We are going to die,” he said to his wife, “for we have seen God!”

But his wife replied, “If the LORD had intended to kill us, He would not have accepted the burnt offering and the grain offering from our hands, nor would He have shown us all these things or spoken to us this way.”

units.label: The birth of Samson and the stirring of the Spirit

verses.text: So the woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him.
And the {{ruach|Spirit}} of the LORD began to stir him at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.

malak.gloss: Messenger, angel. The Angel of the LORD in this chapter is no ordinary messenger: He accepts a burnt offering, does a marvelous thing, ascends in the flame, and is finally identified with God Himself, so that Manoah cries, we have seen God. Many read this as a Christophany, an appearing of the eternal Son before His incarnation.

nazir.gloss: A Nazirite, one separated or consecrated to God, marked by not cutting the hair, avoiding wine and grape products, and shunning defilement, Numbers 6. Samson is a Nazirite from the womb until death, set apart by God before he is even conceived, a living sign that his whole life belongs to the LORD and to His saving purpose.

pele.gloss: Wonder, marvel; the root behind the Angel's answer that His name is beyond comprehension, or wonderful. The very same word names the coming Messiah in Isaiah 9:6, Wonderful Counselor. The visitor who bears an unsearchable, wonderful name and ascends in the flame reveals the God whose ways are past finding out.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, wind, breath. The Spirit of the LORD who begins to stir Samson is the same Spirit who empowered the earlier judges, the source of the strength and courage by which God will work deliverance. That God's own Spirit moves the child marks Samson's rescue of Israel as God's work, not merely human might.

basic.context: Israel does evil once more, and God hands them to the Philistines for forty years. Strikingly, no cry for rescue is recorded; the people seem too settled in their oppression even to call out. Yet God acts anyway. The Angel of the LORD comes to a barren woman, the wife of Manoah of Dan, and promises her a son who is to be a Nazirite from the womb, set apart to begin delivering Israel. Manoah prays for the visitor to return, and He does, repeating the instructions. When they prepare an offering, the Angel does a marvelous thing and ascends in the altar flame, and the couple realize they have seen God. In time the woman bears Samson, the LORD blesses him, and the Spirit of the LORD begins to stir him.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, told with reverence and wonder, and its heart is God's gracious initiative. We should not reduce it to a lesson on parenting or turn the mysterious visitor into a mere angel; the text presses us toward awe, and toward the God who stoops to save. The Nazirite instructions are specific to Samson and his calling, not a rule for all believers. The abiding truths are God's sovereign grace, His power to give life where there was barrenness, and His faithfulness to raise a deliverer even for an undeserving people.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on four words. The visitor is the malak, the Angel of the LORD, who proves to be God Himself. The child is a nazir, a Nazirite, consecrated to God from the womb. When Manoah asks the Angel's name, He says it is pele, wonderful, beyond comprehension, the very word Isaiah uses of the Messiah. And at the end the ruach, the Spirit of the LORD, begins to stir Samson, marking his deliverance as God's own work.
basic.typology: The miraculous birth announced to a barren woman by a heavenly messenger foreshadows the greater annunciations of Scripture, above all the birth of Jesus. Samson, set apart from the womb to begin saving Israel, points forward to Christ, set apart from eternity to accomplish salvation in full. And the Angel who bears the name Wonderful and ascends in the flame anticipates the Son whose name is Wonderful Counselor, and who ascends to the Father.
basic.christ: The Angel of the LORD here receives worship and sacrifice, does wonders, and is identified with God, yet appears in a form men can see and speak with; many read this as a pre-incarnate appearing of the Son. His name, Wonderful, is the name Isaiah gives the coming Messiah, and His ascent in the flame prefigures the ascension of Christ. Samson himself, the promised child, is a shadow of the true Deliverer: announced before his birth, set apart to God, empowered by the Spirit to begin a rescue that only Jesus completes when He crushes the true enemy and saves His people fully and forever.
basic.god: The great actor in this chapter is God. He is patient and gracious, sending help to a people who no longer even ask for it. He is the Lord of life, opening a barren womb. He is holy and awesome, so that seeing Him makes Manoah fear for his life, yet He is merciful, receiving the offering rather than destroying the worshipers. And He is sovereign over salvation, setting apart and empowering a deliverer by His own Spirit, so that the rescue of Israel is unmistakably His doing.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 6 gives the Nazirite vow that shapes Samson's calling. Genesis 18 and Exodus 3 show earlier appearances of the Angel of the LORD identified with God. Luke 1 records the annunciations to Zechariah and to Mary, echoing this barren-womb promise. And Isaiah 9 names the Messiah Wonderful Counselor, the very name the Angel bears here.
basic.oneStory: As the book of Judges descends toward chaos, God's grace shines all the brighter: unasked, He announces and sets apart a deliverer. Yet Samson will only begin the deliverance; his flawed, unfinished rescue leaves the reader longing for the true Nazirite, the Son whose name is Wonderful, who alone saves His people to the end. This birth is one more step in the story that leads to Bethlehem and the manger.

context.literary: Judges 13 belongs to a recognizable Old Testament scene, the announcement of a barren woman's coming son, and the writer plays it with careful repetition. The promise arrives in nearly identical words three times: to the woman alone in verse 3, repeated by her to Manoah in verse 7, and confirmed again by the visitor Himself in verse 14, so that by the time Samson is born in verse 24 the outcome has already been guaranteed three times over. The woman herself is never named, yet she is the chapter's most perceptive figure. She alone recognizes the visitor as a man of God, exceedingly awesome, verse 6, and she alone reasons rightly in verse 23 that a God who has just received their offering has not come to kill them. Manoah, named at once in verse 2, plays the slower, more anxious counterpart, wanting a name to hold onto, verse 17, and fearing death once the vision ends, verse 22. The scene turns on the Angel's refusal to give His name, verse 18, a withholding the narrative resolves not with a word but with a sight, the ascent in the altar flame, verse 20. The chapter closes with a small geographical notice, between Zorah and Eshtaol, verse 25, the very phrase that will return at Samson's burial in Judges 16:31, so that this hushed and reverent birth narrative frames the whole compromised story to come between two fixed points on the map.
context.historical: The tribe of Dan, to which Manoah belonged, had been allotted territory on the coastal plain but by this period had been squeezed into the hill country around Zorah and Eshtaol, unable to secure the ground Joshua assigned them; the same territorial pressure will later drive part of the tribe to migrate north in search of land, Judges 18:1. The Philistines were relative newcomers to Canaan, a seafaring people who had settled the coastal cities in the generations before this account and who held a decisive military advantage: centuries later, in Saul's day, they still controlled the region's ironworking and forbade Israelite smiths from making swords or spears, 1 Samuel 13:19-20, a monopoly that made forty years of subjection to them entirely plausible. Barrenness in this culture was not simply sad; it could mean the end of a family's name and inheritance, which is why the promise to Manoah's wife is framed first as an answer to disgrace before it is framed as a mission. The burnt offering Manoah prepares on a rock, rather than at a central sanctuary, verse 19, fits the irregular, ad hoc worship typical of this period, before Israel had a settled king or a single fixed altar; Gideon offered a similar meal on a rock to the Angel of the LORD a generation or two earlier, and fire consumed it the same way, Judges 6:19-21.
context.canonical:
The chapter stands in the long line of God giving sons to barren women, Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and it directly anticipates the New Testament annunciations of John the Baptist and of Jesus. The Angel of the LORD, worshiped and identified with God yet distinct enough to be seen and addressed, belongs to the thread of Old Testament appearances that Christians have long understood as unveilings of the pre-incarnate Son. Samson's Spirit-empowered, God-initiated deliverance points forward to the Messiah, the true and final Judge and Savior.

The Angel's refusal to give a name has exact precedent in Genesis 32:29, where Jacob wrestles at Peniel and is told, why do you ask my name, and it recurs, more anxiously, when Gideon meets the same figure and fears he will die for having seen Him face to face, Judges 6:22-23. Manoah's household stands in that same line of ordinary Israelites who stumble into an extraordinary Presence and only realize afterward whom they have entertained. The chapter also sits at a hinge in the book itself: after several judges who were raised in answer to a cry, Samson is the last judge and the first to be announced before any cry is recorded, so that his birth narrative quietly signals both the end of the recurring pattern and the depth of Israel's need for a deliverer who does not depend on the nation asking rightly.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The writer of Judges is working toward the refrain that closes the book, in those days there was no king in Israel, everyone did what was right in his own eyes, Judges 21:25, and the birth of Samson is written to show both why that verdict is true and why it is not the final word. Everything about this chapter departs from the cycle laid down in Judges 2:16-19, sin, oppression, an outcry, and a raised-up judge. Here Israel does not cry out at all, and the writer wants the reader to feel that silence as evidence of how numb the nation had become to its own bondage. Against that numbness he sets a deliberately overwhelming theophany: an angel who twice appears, refuses a name, ascends in fire, and reduces two ordinary Danites to worship. The author intends his hearers, almost certainly Israelites living under or anticipating a king, to see that Israel's rescue has never rested on the nation's own repentance but entirely on the LORD's initiative and His readiness to consecrate a deliverer before that deliverer can do anything at all, even before he is born. The detail that the boy is a Nazirite for life, not for a season as Numbers 6 normally allows, tells the first hearers that this whole life, not merely this one birth, belongs to God's larger purpose to save.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: What is described here, not prescribed, includes the specific menu of the mother's pregnancy diet and the boy's abstinence from every product of the vine and every unclean thing; those were binding on this particular Nazirite before his birth, not a template for raising Christian children today. Likewise the visible theophany itself, an angel who can be watched consuming an offering in fire and ascending, describes an exceptional case rather than a promise that ordinary prayer will produce comparable visions; most of Scripture, including the rest of Judges, shows God working through more ordinary means. What does transfer is the reasoning modeled by Manoah's wife in verse 23. She does not deny that they have seen something dangerous and holy; she instead argues from what God has already done, He accepted our offering, to what He must therefore intend, He would not now destroy us, and that is a pattern of gospel logic believers are meant to imitate whenever fear of judgment threatens to eclipse the evidence of grace already received.

debates.question: Who is the Angel of the LORD in this chapter?

views.label: A created angel representing God
views.case: He is called the angel, a messenger, and speaks and acts on God's behalf; on this reading the fear and worship are directed through the messenger to the God who sent him, and the language of seeing God is the awe of encountering His representative.

views.label: A pre-incarnate appearing of the Son
views.case: He accepts sacrifice, does a marvelous wonder, ascends in the flame, bears the wonderful, unsearchable name, and is expressly identified with God so that Manoah says we have seen God; the weight of the chapter presses beyond a mere creature toward a true theophany, which Christians read as the eternal Son.

debates.bearing: Either way the chapter reveals God graciously present to save; the Christophany reading richly connects the visitor's name, Wonderful, and His ascent in the flame to the Lord Jesus.

debates.question: Why does the text stress that this deliverer is set apart from the womb, and that Israel offered no cry for help?

views.label: To magnify God's sheer initiative and grace
views.case: With no cry recorded, God moves unbidden, choosing and consecrating a deliverer before the child even exists; salvation is shown to arise wholly from God's mercy, not from Israel's repentance or request.

views.label: To mark how deep Israel's decline has become
views.case: That the people no longer even cry out shows they have grown numb and comfortable in their bondage; the broken pattern signals a nation so far gone that only God's unprompted grace can begin to rescue it.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge on grace: the deeper Israel's numbness, the brighter shines a God who saves before He is asked, foreshadowing the gospel in which Christ comes while we are still helpless.

study.originalLanguages: Four more features of the Hebrew reward attention beyond the four words already noted, malak, nazir, pele, and ruach. First, the announcement itself follows a fixed formula, behold, you are pregnant and will bear a son, the identical wording used for Hagar's son in Genesis 16:11; the narrator wants an alert Israelite ear to hear this birth as one more entry in a familiar pattern of divine announcements to women in distress, even though this time the woman is not a servant fleeing but a wife who has done nothing wrong at all. Second, the woman describes the visitor as exceedingly awesome, nora meod, verse 6, using the same adjective, nora, that describes God Himself throughout the Psalms and that is reserved elsewhere in Judges only for the LORD's own deeds; her vocabulary already tells the reader what her theology has not yet caught up to say aloud. Third, the account plays quietly on a single root. The burnt offering Manoah prepares is an olah, literally a thing that goes up, and when the Angel ascends in its flame the verb is the same root, alah, He went up. The offering and the Angel rise together on the very same Hebrew word, so that the ascent looks like an answer to the sacrifice, the flame carrying both the gift and the giver of the promise upward at once. Fourth, the last verse uses a striking, almost physical verb for the Spirit's first movement in the boy: the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him, using a rare verb elsewhere used for a bell's clapper striking or a heart pounding, so that the Spirit's stirring is pictured less like a gentle nudge and more like an insistent, rhythmic knocking that will not be ignored. Even the boy's name carries the theme. Shimshon is built on shemesh, the ordinary Hebrew word for sun, so that Manoah and his wife, without knowing it, name their son little sun in the same chapter where a fiery visitor has just ascended into the sky before their eyes. None of this replaces the four words already named; it surrounds them, showing that the whole chapter's Hebrew, not only its key nouns, is built to make an ordinary birth feel like a burning bush.

typology.type: The barren woman granted a son by promise, Judges 13:2-5
typology.fulfillment: The exact words given to Manoah's wife, you will conceive and give birth to a son, verse 3, are the very words spoken centuries later to Mary, Luke 1:31, and echo the earlier promise to Hagar, Genesis 16:11. Each case removes the child from ordinary human planning and roots him instead in a spoken word of God that precedes conception. The escalation in Christ is total: Samson's mother was barren but not incapable, while Mary conceives with no man at all, so that the pattern first sketched in Judges reaches an entirely unrepeatable fulfillment, a Son given by promise alone.

typology.type: The consecrated life, set apart to God from the womb, Judges 13:5, 7
typology.fulfillment: Samson's whole life, uncut hair, no wine, no grape, no corpse, is claimed for God before he draws breath, a lifelong rather than seasonal Nazirite vow, Numbers 6:1-8. Luke deliberately borrows the same abstinence language for John the Baptist, who will drink neither wine nor strong drink, Luke 1:15, and the angel tells Mary that the child born of her will for that reason be called holy, Luke 1:35. Both children are marked as belonging wholly to God before they can consent to it. The type falls short in that Samson's consecration will later be worn thin and finally surrendered, while the greater Son remains holy without interruption from womb to grave, Hebrews 7:26.

typology.type: The Angel who bears a wonderful, unsearchable name and ascends in fire, Judges 13:18, 20
typology.fulfillment: When Manoah asks a name and is refused one because it is beyond comprehension, verse 18, the text withholds exactly what the reader most wants, forcing worship without a name to hold onto. Isaiah later gives the coming king this same word as a title, Wonderful, Isaiah 9:6, and the New Testament shows the ascended Christ still bearing a name above every name, Philippians 2:9. The ascent in the altar flame anticipates a greater ascent, when the risen Christ goes up before witnesses and is received out of their sight, Acts 1:9. The type is real but partial, since Manoah's visitor ascends and is never seen again in the chapter, while Christ ascends only to return.

typology.type: The Spirit who first stirs the deliverer before any battle is fought, Judges 13:25
typology.fulfillment: The Spirit begins to move Samson at Mahaneh-dan long before he lifts a hand against the Philistines, marking the deliverance as God's initiative from the very start, exactly as the Spirit descends on Jesus at the Jordan before He has preached a word or healed anyone, Luke 3:21-22. In both cases empowerment precedes any recorded work, so the mission itself, not merely its results, is credited to the Spirit. The type breaks down at the point of durability: the Spirit that begins to stir Samson can later depart from him unnoticed, Judges 16:20, while the Spirit rests permanently on Christ, John 1:32-33.

study.christ:
This chapter is unusual among the judge narratives because it holds two separate pictures of Christ side by side without collapsing them into one. On one hand there is the visitor Himself, worshiped, accepting a sacrifice, ascending in fire, and confessed as God, who stands in a line of appearances many readers take as the pre-incarnate Son making Himself known before Bethlehem, Genesis 18:1-2 and Exodus 3:2-6 among them. On the other hand there is the child who is promised, set apart, and later empowered by the Spirit, who points not to the Son's eternal being but to His mission as a Deliverer still to come. Judges 13 therefore lets the reader watch, in a single scene, both what the Son already is and what a Deliverer must one day do.

The chapter's emotional turn is worth lingering over. Manoah cries, we are going to die, for we have seen God, verse 22, the ordinary and correct fear of a sinner in the presence of holiness. His wife's answer, that the LORD who has just accepted their burnt offering has no intention of destroying them, is gospel logic in miniature: safety is read off an accepted sacrifice, not off their own worthiness. That is exactly the argument Hebrews will later make explicit, that believers may now draw near with confidence, not because they have earned it, but because of the blood of Jesus which opens a new and living way, Hebrews 10:19-20. Manoah trembled at an animal's blood on a rock; the writer of Hebrews invites us to draw near because of a better blood already shed once for all.

Finally, the whole announcement is unrequested. No cry for help opens this chapter, unlike every earlier judge cycle, and yet God moves first anyway, choosing and naming a deliverer while Israel is still comfortable in its chains. Paul will later state as doctrine what Judges 13 shows in narrative: God demonstrates His own love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, Romans 5:8. Grace precedes the request in both places, and in both cases it is God who supplies what the guilty could not have thought to ask for.
study.god:
God's initiative in this chapter runs deeper than the bare fact that He speaks before Israel cries. He also, remarkably, repeats Himself. Manoah asks for the visitor to come a second time so that husband and wife might learn together how to raise the boy, verse 8, and God grants a request that a more exacting deity might have refused as unnecessary; the first announcement was already sufficient, yet the LORD condescends again to strengthen weak and anxious faith. That willingness to answer the same promise twice, and to answer a practical question about a child's upbringing, verse 12, shows a God who involves Himself in ordinary domestic detail, not only in grand acts of deliverance.

His refusal to give a name, verse 18, belongs to a wider biblical pattern of a God who will not be fully captured in speech. When Moses asks a similar question at the burning bush, he receives not a proper name so much as a declaration of self-existence, I AM WHO I AM, Exodus 3:14, an answer that reveals without exhausting. Here the word for the refusal, wonderful or beyond comprehension, does the same work: God discloses Himself genuinely, in fire and word, while remaining beyond the reach of a label Manoah could use to summon or control Him. This is holiness as much as it is mystery, a God who can be known and trusted without ever being managed.

The chapter also shows God holding fear and mercy together without letting either cancel the other. Manoah's dread that seeing God must mean dying is not corrected as foolish; it is the right instinct of a sinner before holiness. What corrects it is not a lowering of God's holiness but a right reading of His actions: He does not receive an offering from people He intends to destroy. God, in other words, teaches His people to reason forward from what He has already done to what He must therefore intend, rather than backward from their fear to a verdict about His character.

Finally, God is shown as sovereign over biology itself. A barren womb yields to His word as easily as fire consumes an offering; nothing in Manoah's household, not his wife's condition, not the timing of Philistine oppression, not even the couple's fear, escapes His governing hand. The deliverance that follows, twenty years later, is traced back to this one quiet evening because God, not circumstance, authored it from the start.

crossReferences.note: The angel of the LORD finds another anxious woman, Hagar, alone in the wilderness, promises her a son, and gives instructions for his life before he is born. Hagar names the LORD the God who sees me. Like Manoah's wife, she meets God unannounced and comes away certain she has been seen and cared for.

Jacob wrestles through the night with a mysterious man and asks his name, only to be answered, why do you ask my name, the identical challenge Manoah receives in verse 18. Both encounters end in blessing rather than harm, teaching that an unnamed God can still be a God who blesses.

Earlier in the book this same angel of the LORD confronts all Israel at Bochim over their broken covenant, and the people weep. In chapter 13 he comes instead with an unrequested promise of a deliverer, showing that the messenger who rebukes sin is the same one who initiates grace.

Gideon's meeting with the angel of the LORD follows the same shape as Manoah's, an offering prepared, fire from the rock, terror at having seen God face to face. Gideon is answered with the words peace be with you, and Manoah's wife supplies the same reassurance from the logic of the accepted sacrifice.

The ordinary Nazirite vow was a temporary, self-chosen separation to the LORD, ended by a set of closing sacrifices. Samson's is unique in Scripture for being imposed by God before conception and extended for his entire life, marking his whole existence, not one season of it, as consecrated.

Zechariah receives an angelic promise of a son in circumstances close to Manoah's own, an elderly and barren household, a messenger who appears without warning, instructions about the child's future consecration. Unlike Manoah, Zechariah answers with doubt and is struck silent until the birth confirms the word.

The angel Gabriel greets Mary with words that echo Judges 13 almost exactly, behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son, before naming a mission far greater than Samson's, a kingdom that will never end. The formula that first marks Samson's birth reaches its true weight here.

Isaiah names the coming king Wonderful, the same word the angel uses of himself in Judges 13:18 when he says his name is beyond comprehension. Centuries before Isaiah wrote, this chapter had already let Israel hear that wonderful name spoken by a visitor who could not yet be identified.

Manoah fears death because they have seen God and prepared their sacrifice on a bare rock. Hebrews describes a greater and final access into God's presence, a new and living way opened through the curtain of Christ's body, so that fear before holiness gives way to confidence grounded in a better blood.

Moses asks God's name at the burning bush and receives not a label but a declaration of being, I AM WHO I AM. The angel's answer to Manoah, that his name is beyond comprehension, belongs to the same pattern, a God who reveals Himself truly while remaining greater than any name could hold.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3:15 promised that the seed of the woman would be wounded in the heel while crushing the serpent's head, and by the time Jacob blesses his sons that image has attached itself specifically to Dan: Dan will be a viper in the path that bites the horse's heels, and Jacob immediately breaks off to say, I await your salvation, O LORD, Genesis 49:16-18. It is a striking detail that the deliverer this chapter announces, from the very tribe marked by heel imagery and awaited salvation, is given not after a national cry for help but purely by grace, as if the long wait Jacob voiced were finally being answered on its own timetable rather than Israel's.

The barrenness that opens the chapter also reaches back further than any single judge story. Since Eden, childbirth itself has carried the weight of a curse, Genesis 3:16, and a womb that cannot conceive at all is that curse pressed to its limit, a family line with no future. God's word to Manoah's wife does not lift the curse from the world, but it does what His word alone can do within it: it opens what nature had closed, exactly as it had already done for Sarah, and will do again for Elizabeth, evidence that the line carrying God's promise has never depended on ordinary fertility.

Judges as a whole is spiraling downward, each generation worse than the one before it, Judges 2:19, until by the book's last chapters Israel has no king and does whatever seems right in its own eyes, Judges 21:25. Chapter 13 marks the exact point where God stops waiting on the cycle to repeat and moves first, and the reader is meant to feel both relief and unease: relief that grace still comes, unease that it now must come unasked, because the nation itself has grown too settled in bondage to ask for it. The chapter, in other words, is the hinge between a story of repeated failure and a story that will only be resolved outside the cycle altogether, in a King and a Deliverer who never needs to be prompted by His people's misery to love them.

quiz.q: What is striking about how Israel's oppression is described at the start of this chapter?

options.text: Israel does evil and is handed to the Philistines, but no cry for help is recorded; God moves to save unbidden.
options.note: Unlike the earlier cycles, no cry is mentioned, magnifying God's sheer grace in acting first.

options.text: Israel is oppressed by the Philistines for forty years.
options.note: True, but it misses the pointed absence of any cry for rescue that highlights God's initiative.

options.text: Israel repents deeply and begs God for a deliverer.
options.note: The opposite; no repentance or cry is recorded, which is precisely the point.

options.text: Israel defeats the Philistines on its own.
options.note: Israel is under Philistine domination; it does not defeat them here.

quiz.q: What did the Angel of the LORD announce about the coming child?

options.text: He would be a Nazirite to God from the womb and would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
options.note: Verse 5 gives both the lifelong consecration and the mission to begin Israel's deliverance.

options.text: He would be a specially dedicated son given to a barren woman.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits the Nazirite calling and the mission of deliverance.

options.text: He would become a wealthy and powerful ruler.
options.note: The promise concerns consecration and deliverance, not wealth or a throne.

options.text: He would be an ordinary child with no special calling.
options.note: He is set apart as a Nazirite from the womb, anything but ordinary.

quiz.q: How did Manoah and his wife come to realize who their visitor was?

options.text: The Angel did a marvelous thing and ascended in the altar flame, and they fell facedown, saying they had seen God.
options.note: Verses 19-22 record the wonder, the ascent in the flame, and Manoah's cry that they have seen God.

options.text: The visitor told them plainly that he was God.
options.note: He did not give his name; they realized it through the wonder and the ascent in the flame.

options.text: They guessed because he refused their goat.
options.note: His refusal pointed them to worship God, but the revelation came in the ascending flame.

options.text: They never realized who he was.
options.note: Manoah expressly recognized it was the Angel of the LORD and that they had seen God.

quiz.q: What did the Angel say when Manoah asked His name?

options.text: That His name is beyond comprehension, or wonderful, the very word Isaiah uses of the Messiah.
options.note: Verse 18 gives the wonderful, unsearchable name, tied to Isaiah 9:6, Wonderful Counselor.

options.text: That His name was too holy to be spoken aloud.
options.note: Close in spirit, but the text says His name is wonderful and beyond comprehension, not merely unspeakable.

options.text: That His name was Manoah's to choose.
options.note: The Angel keeps His own name hidden; it is not Manoah's to give.

options.text: That His name was simply Gabriel.
options.note: No such name is given; the Angel says His name is wonderful and beyond comprehension.

quiz.q: How does the birth of Samson point forward to Christ?

options.text: A deliverer announced to a barren woman, set apart from the womb, and stirred by the Spirit foreshadows Christ, announced and set apart to save His people fully.
options.note: The annunciation, consecration, and Spirit-anointing all anticipate Jesus, who completes what Samson only begins.

options.text: It shows God gives special children to accomplish His plans.
options.note: True, but it understates how Samson's calling and the Angel named Wonderful point directly to Christ.

options.text: It teaches that deliverers always succeed perfectly.
options.note: Samson only begins the deliverance and does so flawed, which makes us long for the true Savior.

options.text: It has no real connection to Christ.
options.note: The wonderful Angel and the Spirit-set-apart deliverer clearly point to Christ.

questions: God moved to save Israel before they even cried out. How does it change your view of grace to know that God takes the initiative toward people who are not yet asking?
The Angel's name is Wonderful, beyond comprehension. Where do you need to let God be greater and more mysterious than your understanding of Him, and simply worship?
Manoah's wife reasoned that God would not have received their offering only to destroy them. How can you preach that same gospel logic to your own fearful heart when you feel condemned?
Samson was set apart to God from the womb, his whole life claimed for God's purpose. What would it look like to see your own life as wholly consecrated, belonging to the LORD?
Samson only began a deliverance that Christ completes. How does resting in the finished, unflawed salvation of Jesus free you from looking to flawed deliverers, including yourself?

translationNotes.note: Angel may also be rendered Angel with a capital, and the BSB footnote notes that the corresponding pronouns may be capitalized throughout the chapter, reflecting the widespread reading of this figure as a divine appearance.
Nazirite renders a word the BSB footnote also gives as set apart; a Nazirite, from Numbers 6, was consecrated to God, marked by uncut hair and abstinence from wine and defilement.

Beyond comprehension translates a Hebrew word meaning wonderful or full of wonder; it is the same root behind the Messianic title Wonderful in Isaiah 9:6, which is why many hear an unveiling of the coming Christ here.
Mahaneh-dan, where the Spirit began to stir Samson, means camp of Dan, according to the BSB footnote; it lay between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tribe's territory.
